reason: The sources provide dozens of cross-verified scientific claims detailing the five eras, timelines, and physical mechanisms of the universe's ultimate heat death.
story: Our universe is currently living through the Stelliferous Era, illuminated by hundreds of billions of galaxies. But this stellar era is fleeting. In about one hundred trillion years, star formation will exhaust all remaining interstellar gas. The longest-lived stars, low-mass red dwarfs, will burn through their nuclear fuel and cool into black dwarfs. Over quintillions of years, gravitational encounters will fling most stellar remnants out of merged super-galaxies, leaving isolated supermassive black holes behind. Yet even these black holes cannot endure. Through quantum Hawking radiation, black holes slowly lose mass and radiate energy into the void. As they shrink, their temperatures rise until, around a googol years from now—a one followed by one hundred zeroes—the last black holes will evaporate in final bursts of radiation. The cosmos will enter the eternal Dark Era: a cold, motionless sea of leptons and photons where no energy can ever be harvested again.
angle: In 100 trillion years, all star formation permanently ends, and after a googol years, even supermassive black holes will evaporate away into radiation, leaving the universe completely dark, frozen, and inert forever.

claims.claim: The heat death scenario of the universe is also commonly referred to by astronomers as the Big Chill or Big Freeze.
Current astronomical observations indicate that the expansion of the universe will continue indefinitely.
Observations of distant Type Ia supernovae in 1998 showed that the expansion rate of the universe is accelerating.
Astrophysicists Fred Adams and Gregory Laughlin divided the timeline of an expanding universe into five distinct eras.
The present cosmic era, characterized by active star formation from molecular gas clouds, is named the Stelliferous Era.
Low-mass red dwarf stars are the longest-living stars in the cosmos, possessing lifetimes exceeding 10 trillion years.
In roughly 100 trillion years, the interstellar gas supply will be depleted and all normal star formation will cease.
After exhausting their nuclear fuel, cooled degenerate stellar remnants include white dwarfs that eventually fade into dark black dwarfs.
The Milky Way and Andromeda galaxies will eventually collide and coalesce into a single large merged galaxy.
During the Degenerate Era, dynamical relaxation and close gravitational encounters will eject the vast majority of stellar remnants out of their host galaxies.
If two carbon-oxygen white dwarfs collide with a combined mass exceeding roughly 1.4 solar masses, runaway fusion triggers a Type Ia supernova.
Black holes slowly lose mass and evaporate over time by emitting particles through quantum Hawking radiation.
As a black hole decreases in mass via Hawking radiation, its temperature and rate of emission increase.
During its final seconds of evaporation, a dying black hole emits an energetic burst of radiation.
By approximately 1 googol (10^100) years, even the largest supermassive black holes will have evaporated away.
After black holes evaporate, the universe enters the Dark Era, populated mainly by a dilute gas of photons and leptons.
In full thermodynamic heat death, energy is uniformly distributed, making it impossible to perform physical work or sustain life.
If protons decay over long timescales, nucleons inside white dwarfs and neutron stars will disintegrate into radiation and leptons.

disputed: Proton decay: Grand Unified Theories predict nucleons decay on scales of 10^32 to 10^42 years, but experimental evidence has not confirmed proton instability; if protons are stable, remnants persist vastly longer until quantum tunneling turns them into iron stars (attribute as theoretical condition: 'if protons decay').

Certainty of Milky Way-Andromeda merger: 2012 Hubble tracking suggested a definite collision in 4-5 billion years, but 2025 Gaia and Hubble analysis found only a 50% probability over the next 10 billion years (attribute as 'may merge').

Absolute zero vs. horizon temperature floor: Classical thermodynamics posits cooling to absolute zero, but dark energy with a cosmological constant imposes an event horizon with an asymptotic temperature floor around 2x10^-30 kelvin (attribute as 'approaching near absolute zero').

Permanence of dark energy: Standard Lambda-CDM cosmology assumes a constant dark energy density driving heat death, whereas emerging observations like DESI hint dark energy could vary or decay, possibly enabling a Big Rip, Big Crunch, or vacuum decay (attribute heat death to 'the standard cosmological model').
